title: Loops
subtitle: for, while, range, break, continue, enumerate
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Repeating the same action 1000 times by copying code is impossible. You need a way to repeat actions automatically.
whyItExists.solution: Loops repeat code. for loops iterate over sequences (lists, strings, ranges). while loops repeat until a condition becomes False.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Process every item in a list. Repeat until user enters valid input. Count up or down. Search through data.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: For transforming lists, prefer list comprehensions. For filtering, prefer filter() or comprehensions. Avoid while True loops without a clear break condition.

explainModes.beginner: A for loop visits each item in a sequence one by one. for name in names: does something with each name. A while loop keeps going as long as a condition is True — like a while the kettle isn't boiled, keep waiting.
explainModes.simple: for item in collection: — iterates over any iterable. range(n) generates 0 to n-1. range(start, stop, step). enumerate() gives index + value. while condition: — repeats until False. break exits the loop. continue skips to the next iteration. else on a for/while runs if no break occurred.
explainModes.standard: Python's for loop is really a for-each — it works on any iterable (list, tuple, string, dict, file, generator). for key in dict: iterates over keys; for key, val in dict.items() for pairs. zip() pairs two iterables. range() returns a lazy range object (not a list). while loops: dangerous without a guaranteed termination condition — add a counter limit if uncertain.
explainModes.technical: Python's for loop uses the iterator protocol: calls iter() on the collection to get an iterator, then repeatedly calls next() until StopIteration. for-else and while-else are unique to Python — the else clause runs only if the loop completed normally (no break). This is useful for search patterns: for x in data: if found: break else: not_found(). break and continue only affect the innermost loop.
explainModes.deepDive: Generator expressions and list comprehensions are optimised for-loops. itertools provides advanced iteration tools: chain, cycle, repeat, islice, groupby, product, permutations, combinations. For parallel iteration: zip(), or more_itertools.zip_broadcast(). for is syntactic sugar for the iterator protocol — custom classes can be iterable by implementing __iter__ and __next__.

content.code:
# Iterate over a list
fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']
for fruit in fruits:
    print(fruit)
# apple
# banana
# cherry

# range() — generate a sequence of numbers
for i in range(5):
    print(i)          # 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

for i in range(2, 8):
    print(i)          # 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7

for i in range(0, 10, 2):
    print(i)          # 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 (step=2)

# Iterate over a string
for char in 'Python':
    print(char)       # P, y, t, h, o, n

# enumerate() — index + value at the same time
names = ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie']
for i, name in enumerate(names):
    print(f'{i}: {name}')
# 0: Alice
# 1: Bob
# 2: Charlie

# Start index at 1
for i, name in enumerate(names, start=1):
    print(f'{i}. {name}')   # 1. Alice, 2. Bob...

# zip() — iterate two lists together
scores = [95, 82, 78]
for name, score in zip(names, scores):
    print(f'{name}: {score}')
# Alice: 95 | Bob: 82 | Charlie: 78

questions.question: What does range(2, 8) generate?
questions.explanation: range(start, stop) generates numbers from start up to (but NOT including) stop. range(2, 8) gives 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 — six numbers.

faq.q: How do I loop with both index and value?
faq.a: Use enumerate(): for i, item in enumerate(my_list): gives you i (0-based index) and item simultaneously. To start at 1: enumerate(my_list, start=1). Avoid the C-style: for i in range(len(my_list)): my_list[i] — it works but is un-Pythonic.

faq.q: When should I use while vs for?
faq.a: Use for when you know what you're iterating over (a list, a range, a file). Use while when you're waiting for something to happen (user input, a condition to change, retrying an operation). Prefer for — it's safer (can't accidentally infinite loop on a finite sequence).

examples: for row in csv.reader(f): — process every row in a CSV file
while retries < 3: — retry a failed HTTP request up to 3 times
for i, item in enumerate(items, 1): print(f'{i}. {item}') — numbered lists
